discovery: Discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory
motivation: Francis Halzen conceived and led IceCube, which turned a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice into a telescope and opened a new observational window on the energetic universe. In 2013 IceCube discovered a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos at TeV-PeV energies. It then associated neutrinos with the flaring blazar TXS 0506+056 (2017-18), found evidence for emission from the active galaxy NGC 1068 (2022), and imaged the Galactic plane in neutrinos (2023). Neutrinos travel undeflected and are produced only in hadronic interactions, so these measurements give direct, quantitative evidence of where cosmic rays are accelerated. That long-standing question had previously been approached only indirectly, through photons. For astrophysicists who study cosmic rays, supernova remnants, starbursts and feedback, IceCube made neutrino astronomy a working, multimessenger discipline. It links X-ray, gamma-ray and particle observations into one physical picture.
